newsYesterday.headline: Stock Rotation Hits AI Winners on Spending Worries: Markets Wrap
newsYesterday.blurb: A record plunge in Alphabet on disappointing sales revived doubts over the AI trade and pushed money into a broader set of stocks and into bonds. The Nasdaq 100 lost 1.4%; Microsoft drew blowout demand for a $25bn bond sale; Amazon slumped late as its spending soared; Intel’s revenue forecast missed.

newsYesterday.headline: Alphabet shares tumble in $500bn rout
newsYesterday.blurb: Alphabet fell 13%, a record $500bn loss for the company and the second-biggest one-day drop in Wall Street history after Nvidia’s $593bn in Jan 2025. Search revenue rose 12% to $63.4bn, missing estimates of $64.9bn, as Google admitted “AI mode” queries are eating into traditional search; free cash flow was -$9.1bn and capex $51.3bn. Microsoft beat but its shares slipped 0.2%.

newsYesterday.headline: US tech stocks fall after earnings fuel AI spending concerns
newsYesterday.blurb: Nasdaq 100 -1.4%, S&P 500 -0.3%. Alphabet fell 12.3%; Samsung fell more than 4% in Seoul on weak chip profits; Microsoft invested less than expected in data centres due to construction delays. Treasuries rallied despite strong GDP — partly on lower oil, partly on safety buying — with the 10-year about 0.1 point lower at 4.94%.

newsYesterday.headline: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq slip as Alphabet stock sinks 12% and AI jitters return
newsYesterday.blurb: Live coverage: Alphabet down nearly 13%; Eli Lilly +6% on GLP-1 sales; Intel guided Q4 revenue to $15–16bn vs $17bn expected; Amazon fell as much as 10% after hours before trimming losses, keeping 2026 capex at $220bn. Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% annualised rate; PCE inflation 3.6%, core 3.1%.

newsYesterday.headline: Christine Lagarde to step down as ECB president in February
newsYesterday.blurb: Lagarde will leave on Feb 7, nine months early, announcing it hours before the ECB held rates at 2.5%. She hinted at a hike at the Dec 17 meeting. Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos are seen as front-runners.

newsYesterday.headline: US economy beats forecasts to grow at 3.4% rate in third quarter
newsYesterday.blurb: Growth beat the 3.2% Bloomberg forecast and Q2’s 2.2%. Private fixed investment jumped 9.4%, the most since 2020, on AI spending; consumer spending rose 3.8%. PCE inflation rose to 3.6% from 3.4%.

glossary.def: A basket of company shares, like the S&P 500. Its level tells you how the whole basket is doing.
The price of borrowing money, set mainly by the central bank. Higher rate = more expensive to borrow.
The return for lending to a government. When yields rise, bond prices fall, and safe lending competes with stocks.
One hundredth of a percentage point. A yield going from 4.93% to 5.05% has risen 12 bp.
How fast everyday prices rise. High inflation is why central banks raise rates.
The extra yield a riskier borrower pays over a safer one (e.g. France over Germany). Wider = more perceived risk.
Insurance against a borrower defaulting, quoted in bp per year. Higher = more worry.
Expected volatility of US stocks (VIX) and of US Treasury yields (MOVE): the markets' fear gauges.
How many stocks are actually rising, not just the index average. Compare the S&P 500 with its equal-weight version.
The forecast economists expect before a data release. Markets move on the gap between the actual number and the consensus.
Hawkish: leaning to higher rates to fight inflation. Dovish: leaning to lower rates to support growth and jobs.
The policy rate minus inflation. Only a clearly positive real rate is truly restrictive.
The 10-year yield minus the 2-year. Steepening: the gap widens. Flattening: it narrows.
Bigger companies count for more. The S&P 500 is cap-weighted; the Dow is price-weighted.

simpleYesterday.bigPicture: Big Tech had a bad day. Alphabet (Google) lost a record $500bn in value after saying its new AI search mode is eating into its old search business, and Amazon and Intel fell after hours. Investors moved money out of tech and into government bonds, so US borrowing costs fell — the 10-year yield dropped back below 5%. That happened even though the economy grew faster than expected (3.4%) and inflation rose to 3.6%, and markets still expect the Fed to raise rates in December. In Europe stocks rose, the ECB held rates and Christine Lagarde said she will step down early. Oil stayed above $100 as the US weighs new strikes on Iran after next week’s elections.

chain.explanation: Disappointing results from the biggest AI spenders pushed investors out of tech and into the safety of bonds, so stock prices and bond yields both fell.

driverNotes.equities: The Nasdaq fell 1.38% to 26,184.72, the S&P 500 0.31% to 7,720.22 and the Dow 0.25% to 52,342.56, while small caps rose 0.96%. Why: Alphabet fell 12–13% — a record $500bn loss of value — after weaker search revenue and admitting AI search is eating into its core business (FT); Samsung also fell more than 4% on weak chip profits (FT). Impact: money rotated into other parts of the market (Eli Lilly +6%, Yahoo Finance) and Europe rose (DAX +1.31%). After the close Amazon fell as much as 10% and Intel about 16% (Yahoo Finance, FT), which could weigh on Friday’s open.
driverNotes.fixedIncome: US yields fell: 10-year -11.7bp to 4.934% and 30-year to 5.298% (watchlist), with the 2-year near 4.6–4.65%. Why: the FT said bonds rallied despite strong GDP, partly on a lower oil price and as investors sought safety from AI stocks. Impact: inflation is still rising (PCE 3.6%) and markets priced an 83.5% chance of a December hike after the Fed meeting (CME FedWatch via Investing.com), so the rally could reverse. In Europe the ECB held at 2.5% and hinted at a December hike (FT); France’s 10-year fell to 4.910%.
driverNotes.others: Watchlist Brent $111.49 and WTI $102.86 were little changed after Wednesday’s jump. The WSJ reported the US told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign against Iran after Nov 3 (via FT), and also reported new US outreach to Tehran (via Yahoo Finance). European gas topped €100/MWh on Oct 28 for the first time since 2022 (FT) before easing to €98.55. Gold fell 1.13% to $4,021.39, silver 3.35% and Bitcoin 2.28% to $79,524.

forces.title: Why Alphabet’s Fall Shook the Whole Market
forces.analogy: Like a star chef admitting the new menu is stealing customers from the old one — diners wonder whether all the money spent on the new kitchen will pay off.
forces.explanation: Alphabet’s search revenue grew 12% to $63.4bn, missing estimates, and Google admitted its “AI mode” answers are eating into traditional search ads. It also burned $9.1bn of cash as AI capex hit $51.3bn in the quarter. The shares fell about 13%, wiping out roughly $500bn — a record for Alphabet and the second-biggest one-day loss in Wall Street history.
forces.source: Financial Times — “Alphabet shares tumble in $500bn rout” (Oct 29, 2026)
forces.whyItMatters: If AI starts eating the profits of existing businesses before it earns its own, investors may demand less spending — bad news for chipmakers and data-centre builders.

forces.title: Why Yields Fell Even With a Strong Economy
forces.analogy: Like people running into a shop to get out of the rain — they’re not there because the shop is great, they just want shelter.
forces.explanation: The economy grew at a 3.4% pace in Q3 and PCE inflation rose to 3.6%, which would normally push yields up. But when tech stocks fell, investors bought government bonds for safety, and a lower oil price helped too (FT), pushing the 10-year yield down to about 4.93%.
forces.source: Financial Times — “US economy beats forecasts to grow at 3.4% rate”; “US tech stocks fall after earnings fuel AI spending concerns” (Oct 29, 2026)
forces.whyItMatters: Lower yields make borrowing cheaper, but with an 83.5% chance of a December hike priced in, a fear-driven bond rally can reverse quickly.

forces.title: Why Oil Stays Above $100
forces.analogy: Like a forecast of a storm next week — nothing has happened yet, but people still stock up.
forces.explanation: The WSJ reported that the US told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense military campaign against Iran after the Nov 3 midterms, and the FT reports Israel’s inconclusive election leaves Netanyahu free to join one. At the same time there is new diplomacy, so prices are high but not rising every day.
forces.source: FT — “European gas prices jump above €100…” (Oct 28) and “Israel vote leaves door open to Iran attack” (Oct 29); The National (Oct 28)
forces.whyItMatters: Expensive oil keeps inflation high, which is one reason the Fed may still raise rates in December.

glossary.def: A big basket of company shares, like the S&P 500. Its price tells you how the whole basket is doing, not just one company.
The “price” of borrowing money. Set mainly by the Fed (the U.S. central bank). Higher rate = more expensive to borrow.
The return you get for lending money to a government. When yields rise, “safe” lending pays better — which can pull money away from stocks.
How fast prices for everyday things are rising. High inflation is why the Fed raises interest rates.
The extra interest a borrower (like France) pays compared with a safer borrower (like Germany) for a same-length loan. A wider spread means investors see more risk in that borrower.

How many stocks in an index are actually rising, not just the index's overall average. 'Narrow' breadth means a few big stocks (like AI chipmakers) are doing all the work while most others lag or fall.
Insurance on a loan. The buyer pays a yearly fee and gets paid if the borrower can't repay. A higher CDS price means investors are more worried about that borrower.
When a central bank hints at what it will do next with interest rates. Fed Chair Warsh says he won’t give it except in a crisis, so markets have to guess more.
The giant cloud companies — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta — that spend hundreds of billions on data centres for AI. Their results move the whole AI trade.

lessons.title: Markets trade the surprise, not the level
lessons.text: Investors already expect a number (the consensus). Prices move on the gap between the actual and that expectation.
lessons.today: BoE MPC Vote Rate Hike: 9 vs 7 expected (hawkish surprise).

lessons.title: Growth stocks behave like long bonds
lessons.text: Most of a growth company's value sits in profits far in the future. When rates or confidence change, those distant cash flows swing the most.

lessons.title: Flight to quality
lessons.text: In a scare, money leaves risky assets for safe ones: Treasuries rally (yields fall), and the dollar, yen, Swiss franc and gold tend to firm.

lessons.title: Supply shocks are the hardest case
lessons.text: An oil shock pushes inflation up and growth down at the same time, leaving central banks with no good option.

library.title: Markets trade the surprise, not the level
library.text: Investors already expect a number (the consensus). Prices move on the gap between the actual and that expectation.

library.title: Two channels: cash flows and the discount rate
library.text: Every headline reaches prices through expected profits, the discount rate, or both. A strong jobs report can lift profits and yields at the same time: the net effect decides.

library.title: Good news can be bad news
library.text: When inflation is the main worry, strong data raises the odds of higher rates, and stocks can fall on it.

library.title: In a cap-weighted index, the giants decide
library.text: A handful of mega-caps make up a large share of the S&P 500. The index can fall on a day when most of its stocks rise, and the reverse.

library.title: The Dow is price-weighted
library.text: The Dow weights companies by share price, not size. A few high-priced stocks can push it the other way from the S&P 500.

library.title: Growth stocks behave like long bonds
library.text: Most of a growth company's value sits in profits far in the future. When rates or confidence change, those distant cash flows swing the most.

library.title: One company's revenue is another's cost
library.text: The AI build-out helps the sellers of chips and memory and squeezes the buyers. 'Tech' is not one block.

library.title: Markets hate uncertainty more than bad news
library.text: Fear spikes when the outcome is unknown; once it is known, volatility often fades even if the news is bad.

library.title: Flight to quality
library.text: In a scare, money leaves risky assets for safe ones: Treasuries rally (yields fall), and the dollar, yen, Swiss franc and gold tend to firm.

library.title: Supply shocks are the hardest case
library.text: An oil shock pushes inflation up and growth down at the same time, leaving central banks with no good option.

library.title: Look at real rates
library.text: Policy is only tight if the rate is well above inflation. Rate minus inflation tells you how restrictive the central bank really is.

library.title: Results versus expectations, and guidance
library.text: A company can beat estimates and still fall if the outlook disappoints: prices follow the future, not last quarter.

library.title: Short term: headlines. Long term: profits
library.text: Over days, prices move on fear and news. Over years, they follow earnings.

library.title: Read the curve, not only the level
library.text: If the 2-year moves most, the market is changing its view on the central bank. If the 30-year moves most, it is about inflation, growth or fiscal risk.
